title: After Aurora Temple Plot, Indian Americans Urged to Answer Hate With Votes
excerpt: A jammed rifle stopped an alleged attack in Illinois. Writers and researchers say rising online hate makes civic participation, temple security and turnout on November 3 essential.
body:
• A 19-year-old suspect allegedly tried to open fire at the Sri Venkateswara Swami Temple in Aurora, Illinois, on October 11; his rifle jammed and a co-worker alerted police.
  • Researchers counted about 542,000 posts expressing hatred of South Asians on X between January 2025 and June 2026, with monthly volume up about 240 percent from early 2024.
  • About 2.6 million Indian Americans are eligible to vote, and 92 percent of registered voters in the 2026 AAPI survey said they plan to vote on November 3.
  • Readers can check registration, vote early where available, and ask candidates about temple security grants and hate-crime prevention before November 3.

On Sunday, October 11, thousands of families gathered at the Sri Venkateswara Swami (Balaji) Temple in Aurora, Illinois, to celebrate the start of Navaratri. Among them were Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi and his family. According to prosecutors, a 19-year-old man in body armor was waiting in the parking lot with an AR-style rifle, tried to open fire, and his weapon jammed.

Writing in IndiaWest, Ajay Jain Bhutoria said the suspect later told a co-worker he planned to return, that co-worker called 911, and police arrested him before he could try again. A separate account in Thoughtful India, citing prosecutors and WBEZ Chicago, said Alexandros Paporakis of Palatine had been planning a mass shooting for about two years and had settled on the Aurora temple roughly two months earlier. Police searching his apartment found a rifle, magazines, about 300 rounds of ammunition and an eight-page manifesto.

From online hate to real-world risk

Both accounts place Aurora in a wider pattern. Bhutoria wrote that prosecutors say the suspect's manifesto described people of Indian ancestry, Jews and Black Americans as "subhumans," and that community leaders told the Associated Press the plot was fueled by hateful rhetoric online. Thoughtful India cited the Center for the Study of Organized Hate, which counted roughly 542,000 posts expressing hatred of South Asians on X between January 2025 and June 2026. The Network Contagion Research Institute found anti-Indian discourse on the platform nearly tripled in 2025 and drew more than 300 million views.

"Luck is not a security policy."

— Ajay Jain Bhutoria, IndiaWest

Other incidents cited include bricks thrown through the windows of a Hindu temple in Richmond Heights, Ohio, while worshippers were inside, and gunfire last year at a Krishna temple in Spanish Fork, Utah. In the Carnegie Endowment's 2026 survey of Indian Americans, cited by Thoughtful India, about half of respondents said they had faced discrimination since the start of 2025, roughly one in four said they had been called a slur, and nine percent said they had been physically threatened.

Why civic participation is the response being urged

The argument in both pieces is that professional success alone does not provide protection. Bhutoria noted that, according to the Pew Research Center, the median income of Indian American households is about twice the national median, while many families remain stuck for decades in the green card backlog. Thoughtful India drew lessons from Irish, Chinese, Italian, Japanese and Jewish Americans, and from Sikh Americans after the 2012 Oak Creek gurdwara shooting, arguing that the communities that recovered built professional institutions, public festivals and working relationships with police and local government before a crisis arrived.

For Indian Americans, that translates into practical local work: serving on library boards, park districts, school councils and police advisory committees, building temple security plans, and voting in the local elections that decide who runs those institutions.

Where the vote could matter on November 3

The Carnegie Endowment estimates roughly 2.6 million Indian Americans are eligible to vote. In the 2026 AAPI Voter Survey by APIAVote and AAPI Data, 92 percent of Indian American registered voters said they plan to vote this November and 74 percent said they are absolutely certain they will. Bhutoria pointed to Arizona's 1st Congressional District, metro Atlanta and Gwinnett County in Georgia, California, New Jersey and Pennsylvania as places where suburban Indian American turnout could affect close House and Senate races.

The survey found about 66 percent of Indian American voters prefer the Democratic candidate in their House race, according to the IndiaWest piece. Bhutoria urged readers to check registration, make a plan to vote early or on November 3, bring family and first-time voters, and press candidates on temple safety.

What happens next

The Aurora suspect has been ordered detained on charges of making a terrorist threat and possessing a firearm illegally, according to Thoughtful India, and Krishnamoorthi has asked the FBI to investigate the attempt as a hate crime.
